topic.title: Inverse Functions
topic.summary: When a function is invertible, how an inverse reverses input-output pairs, composition with the identity function, domains and ranges of inverses, reflecting a graph over y = x, and finding an inverse analytically.

lesson.title: Inverse Functions
lesson.summary: When a function is invertible, how an inverse reverses input-output pairs, composition with the identity function, domains and ranges of inverses, reflecting a graph over y = x, and finding an inverse analytically.
learningGoals: 2.8.A Determine the input-output pairs of the inverse of a function.
2.8.B Determine the inverse of a function on an invertible domain.
lesson.bigIdea: An inverse function runs a function backward: it sends each output back to the one input that produced it. That only works when no output comes from two different inputs, which sometimes requires restricting the domain.
lesson.context: Topic 2.7 introduced composition and the identity function. Inverses are defined by composition, and Topic 2.10 uses them to build logarithmic functions as inverses of exponential functions.

sections.title: 2.8.A · A function is invertible if each output comes from a unique input.

blocks.text: On a specified domain, a function, f, has an inverse function, or is invertible, if each output value of f is mapped from a unique input value. The domain of a function may be restricted in many ways to make the function invertible.

An inverse function can be thought of as a reverse mapping of the function. An inverse function, f⁻¹, maps the output values of a function, f, on its invertible domain to their corresponding input values; that is, if f(a) = b, then f⁻¹(b) = a. Alternately, on its invertible domain, if a function consists of input-output pairs (a, b), then the inverse function consists of input-output pairs (b, a).
Example: f(x) = x² is not invertible on all real numbers, because f(−3) = f(3) = 9. Restricted to x ≥ 0, each output comes from one input, and f⁻¹(x) = √x.

sections.takeaway: Invertible means no output is shared; the inverse swaps every (a, b) to (b, a).

sections.title: 2.8.B · A function composed with its inverse is the identity function.

blocks.text: The composition of a function, f, and its inverse function, f⁻¹, is the identity function; that is, f(f⁻¹(x)) = f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.

On a function's invertible domain, the function's range and domain are the inverse function's domain and range, respectively. The inverse of the table of values of y = f(x) can be found by reversing the input-output pairs; that is, (a, b) corresponds to (b, a).

blocks.caption: A table of values of f and the table of its inverse

blocks.title: Write it like the AP Exam

sections.takeaway: f(f⁻¹(x)) = f⁻¹(f(x)) = x, and the domain and range trade places.

sections.title: 2.8.B · Find an inverse by reflecting the graph or reversing the operations.

blocks.text: The inverse of the graph of the function y = f(x) can be found by reversing the roles of the x- and y-axes; that is, by reflecting the graph of the function over the graph of the identity function h(x) = x.

blocks.caption: f(x) = 3x + 5 and its inverse f⁻¹(x) = (x − 5)/3, reflections of each other over y = x
blocks.alt: A steep line f through (0, 5) and (−1, 2), a dashed shallow line through (5, 0) and (2, −1), and a dashed gray line y = x between them. Each point (a, b) on f matches a point (b, a) on the inverse.

blocks.text: The inverse of the function can be found by determining the inverse operations to reverse the mapping. One method for finding the inverse of the function f is reversing the roles of x and y in the equation y = f(x), then solving for y = f⁻¹(x).

blocks.title: Write it like the AP Exam
blocks.text: y = 3x + 5. Reverse the roles of x and y: x = 3y + 5. Solve: y = (x − 5)/3. So f⁻¹(x) = (x − 5)/3.
In addition to limiting the domain of a function to obtain an inverse function, contextual restrictions may also limit the applicability of an inverse function.

sections.takeaway: Swap x and y, then solve for y. The graph reflects over y = x.

connections.title: Preimages
connections.body: Topic 1.1 defined the preimage of an output value as the set of inputs that give it. A function is invertible exactly when every preimage contains a single input.
connections.transferQuestion: If f(2) = f(7) = 10, can f be invertible on a domain containing 2 and 7?
connections.feedback: No. The preimage of 10 contains two inputs, so f⁻¹(10) would not be a single value.

connections.title: Logarithms undo exponentials
connections.body: Topic 2.10 shows that f(x) = log_b x is the inverse of g(x) = bˣ, so the point (s, t) on bˣ becomes (t, s) on log_b x.
connections.transferQuestion: The point (3, 8) is on the graph of y = 2ˣ. What point is on the graph of its inverse?
connections.feedback: (8, 3), because the inverse reverses each input-output pair.
